summary: In the temple courts, Jesus warns the crowds and His disciples against the scribes and Pharisees, pronounces woes on their hypocrisy, and laments over Jerusalem.
key_insight: This is not only a speech against Pharisees. Luke says Jesus spoke “to His disciples” in the hearing of all the people, and in Matthew, before a single woe, He turns to them: “But you, do not be called ‘Rabbi’.” The sins He exposes are the ones that tempt anyone who leads God’s people.
story: Still teaching in the temple, Jesus spoke to the multitudes and to His disciples. {Mt} All the people could hear Him. {Lk} “The scribes and the Pharisees sit in Moses’ seat,” He said. Whatever they taught from the Law, the people should observe and do, “but do not do according to their works; for they say, and do not do.” They tied heavy burdens on other men’s shoulders and would not lift a finger to move them. {Mt}

Everything they did was done to be seen. They made their phylacteries broad and the borders of their garments long. {Mt} “Beware of the scribes, who desire to go around in long robes,” He warned. {Mk} They loved greetings in the marketplaces and the best seats in the synagogues and at feasts. They devoured widows’ houses and covered it with long prayers. “These will receive greater condemnation.” {Mk}

Then He turned to His own followers. “But you, do not be called ‘Rabbi’; for One is your Teacher, the Christ, and you are all brethren.” They were to call no one on earth their father, for they had one Father in heaven. “But he who is greatest among you shall be your servant.” {Mt}

Then came the woes. “Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites!” They shut the kingdom of heaven against men, neither going in nor letting others in. They traveled land and sea to win one convert and made him twice as much a son of hell as themselves. As blind guides, they ruled that an oath by the temple meant nothing but an oath by its gold was binding. They tithed even mint and anise and cummin but neglected “the weightier matters of the law: justice and mercy and faith.” They strained out a gnat and swallowed a camel. {Mt}

They cleaned the outside of the cup and dish while the inside was full of extortion and self-indulgence. They were like whitewashed tombs, beautiful outside and full of dead men’s bones within. They built tombs for the prophets and said they would never have shed the prophets’ blood as their fathers did, and so they testified that they were those fathers’ sons. “Serpents, brood of vipers! How can you escape the condemnation of hell?” He would send them prophets, wise men and scribes, and they would kill and persecute them, until all the righteous blood shed on the earth, from Abel to Zechariah, came upon this generation. {Mt}

Then He spoke to the city itself: “O Jerusalem, Jerusalem, the one who kills the prophets and stones those who are sent to her! How often I wanted to gather your children together, as a hen gathers her chicks under her wings, but you were not willing! See! Your house is left to you desolate.” They would not see Him again until they said, “Blessed is He who comes in the name of the LORD!” {Mt}
differences: Mark and Luke give only a short warning against the scribes: their long robes, love of honor, and long prayers that cover the devouring of widows’ houses. Matthew gives a full discourse and names both “the scribes and the Pharisees.”
Matthew says Jesus spoke “to the multitudes and to His disciples”; Luke says He spoke to His disciples “in the hearing of all the people.”
Only Matthew records the woes and the lament over Jerusalem. Luke gives similar woes earlier, at a Pharisee’s table (Luke 11:37–52), and a similar lament on the journey to Jerusalem (Luke 13:34–35).
The woe about devouring widows’ houses stands in Matthew 23:14 in the NKJV, though some manuscripts of Matthew do not have it there; Mark and Luke both include the saying.

fit.question: Matthew sets the lament “O Jerusalem, Jerusalem” in the temple during Jesus’ last week. Luke gives almost the same words earlier, on the journey to Jerusalem (Luke 13:34–35). When did Jesus say it?

points.label: Said more than once
points.text: A traveling teacher repeated his central sayings, and Jesus’ grief over Jerusalem ran through His whole ministry. In Luke He has not yet reached the city; in Matthew He stands in its temple. The wording differs slightly in the two places.

points.label: Two horizons
points.text: In Luke, “you shall not see Me until” looks ahead to the crowds who would soon hail Him with the words of Psalm 118:26 at the Triumphal Entry (Luke 19:38). In Matthew, spoken after the entry, the same words look past the cross to His return.

points.label: Arranged by subject
points.text: Others think one writer placed the saying where it fit his teaching, since the Gospels do not always follow strict time order.

fit.note: Whether Jesus said it twice or one writer grouped it by theme, nothing here requires an error, and the words themselves agree.
fit.short: Jesus likely lamented over Jerusalem more than once: on the journey (Luke) and again in the temple after His entry (Matthew).

fit.question: Matthew calls the murdered Zechariah “son of Berechiah.” But the Zechariah stoned in the temple court was “the son of Jehoiada” (2 Chronicles 24:20–22), and “Zechariah the son of Berechiah” was the prophet (Zechariah 1:1). Whom did Jesus mean?

points.label: The priest stoned in the temple court
points.text: Most think Jesus meant the Zechariah stoned “in the court of the house of the LORD,” whose death fits “between the temple and the altar” exactly. Chronicles stands last in the traditional Hebrew order, so the list runs from the first martyr in Scripture to the last.

points.label: Son or grandson
points.text: Jehoiada died at 130 (2 Chronicles 24:15), so he may have been Zechariah’s grandfather, with Berechiah his father. Scripture often uses “son” for a descendant: the prophet Zechariah is called both “the son of Berechiah” and “the son of Iddo,” who was his grandfather (Zechariah 1:1; Ezra 5:1).

points.label: The prophet himself
points.text: Others think Jesus meant the prophet Zechariah, whose death Scripture does not record. In a similar saying, Luke names only “Zechariah” (Luke 11:51).

fit.note: The details are not fully settled, but Scripture’s own use of “son” for a grandson shows that the name need not be a mistake.
fit.short: Most think Jesus meant the Zechariah stoned in the temple court, the Hebrew Bible’s last martyr; “son of” can mean grandson.

scene.label: Moses’ seat
scene.text: The scribes read and explained the Law given through Moses, so when they taught it faithfully they spoke with his authority. Stone seats of honor found in later synagogues, such as one at Chorazin, suggest the phrase may also have named an actual chair.

scene.label: Phylacteries and borders
scene.text: Phylacteries were small leather boxes holding Scripture passages, tied to the forehead and arm for prayer, from a literal reading of Deuteronomy 6:8. The “borders” were the tassels God commanded on the corners of every Israelite’s garment (Numbers 15:38–39). Jesus objects not to them, but to enlarging them to be noticed.

scene.label: Proselytes
scene.text: A proselyte was a Gentile who fully converted to Judaism, taking on circumcision and the whole Law. Such converts were known across the Roman world; Acts mentions them in Jerusalem at Pentecost and among the first deacons (Acts 2:10; 6:5). Jesus does not fault the zeal to win them, but what they were won to.

scene.label: A gnat and a camel
scene.text: Careful Jews strained their wine through cloth to avoid swallowing a tiny unclean insect (Leviticus 11:20–23). The camel was the largest unclean animal in the land (Leviticus 11:4). The picture is meant to be absurd.

scene.label: “Rabbi”
scene.text: The word means “my master,” and John translates it “Teacher” (John 1:38). In Jesus’ day it was becoming an honored title for teachers of the Law, and being greeted with it in public was a mark of standing. Jesus tells His disciples to leave the title to Him.

witnesses.matthew: Gives the whole discourse, the last public teaching of Jesus in his Gospel; next, Jesus leaves the temple and speaks of its fall (24:1–2). Writing for readers who knew the scribes and Pharisees well, Matthew shows the King judging Israel’s teachers while still longing to gather Jerusalem’s children.
witnesses.mark: Keeps only a short warning. Just before it, Jesus told one scribe, “You are not far from the kingdom of God” (12:34), so Mark’s warning targets a kind of religion, not every scribe.
witnesses.luke: Gives the same short warning, spoken to the disciples while the people listened, having already recorded fuller woes at a Pharisee’s table (11:37–52). Luke notices widows often (2:37; 7:12; 18:3; 21:2), and here the charge of devouring widows’ houses carries special weight.

seeing.reveals: Jesus speaks as the one Teacher and the Lord of the temple, with authority to pronounce woe on Israel’s teachers. Yet the same voice ends with “How often I wanted to gather your children together.” His judgment comes from a heart that longed to shelter the very people who refused Him.
seeing.living: Jesus’ warnings aim at the gap between saying and doing, and at faith kept up to be seen. Let Him search the places where your religion is worn on the outside: titles, appearances, small rules kept while justice and mercy are neglected. Then take the low place He commands: “he who is greatest among you shall be your servant.”
seeing.ponder: What part of your faith do you keep polished on the outside, and will you let Jesus cleanse the inside?

preaching.big_idea: Jesus exposes religion done to be seen, yet longs to gather the very people He warns.
outline: Teachers who say and do not do (1–7)
The servant way for Jesus’ disciples (8–12)
preaching.watch_for: Jesus’ first great sermon in Matthew opens with blessings (5:3–12); His last public teaching is full of woes. Watch also the word “blind,” used five times (vv. 16, 17, 19, 24, 26): the leaders knew the Law well but could not see its weightier matters.
